Code check

Every measured item meets the ADA figures. 9 pass, 4 to confirm on site. Code mode is off, so nothing was forced.

  • PassSlope 1:12 or gentlerYours is 1:12.
  • PassNo more than 30″ of rise in one runThe longest run rises 12″.
  • PassTurning landing at least 60″ × 60″Your platform is 5′ × 5′ clear inside the curbs.
  • CheckLevel landing at least 60″ deep at the bottomCheck on site. The ground at the foot of the ramp needs to be level and firm for 60″.
  • CheckLevel landing at least 60″ deep at the topCheck on site. Where the ramp meets the door or deck there must be a level area at least 60″ deep and as wide as the door, with room to swing it.
  • PassClear width at least 36″Yours is 42″ between the curbs.
  • PassHandrails on both sidesRails are on both sides of every run.
  • PassHandrail 34″ to 38″ above the deckRails are built at 36″.
  • PassRail extends 12″ past each endBuilt in, 12″ past the top and bottom of every run.
  • PassRail is 4″ to 6¼″ around and no more than 2¼″ acrossA 2x2 is 1½″ by 1½″, a little under 6″ around once its corners are rounded over.
  • PassEdge protection, 2″ minimum curb2x4 curbs on edge stand 3½″ above the deck on both sides.
  • CheckFirm, slip-resistant surfaceCover the whole deck with grit tape, grit paint or rubber matting.
  • CheckCross slope no steeper than 1:48Set the deck level from side to side when you build. No more than ¼″ of fall across 12″.

Based on the common figures in the 2010 ADA Standards (section 405) and the residential ramp rules. Local codes differ, and a home ramp may not need to meet the ADA, but a contractor usually builds to it. Confirm with your building department.

Assembly guide

How to use this guide
  • Do the steps in order. Each step starts with a checklist: what to cut, then how to put it together. Below the checklist, open Boards to cut to see which board each piece comes from. The parts list under it gives every length.
  • Boards to cut says which board to grab. “2x6 #1, 16′ board” means take a 16-foot 2x6 and write #1 on it, then cut the pieces listed beside it. ×4 means cut 4 of that piece.
  • Write each piece’s name on it in pencil as you cut it, like “Ramp 2 Leg 2”. The drawings use the same names and colors.
  • When a step says to keep the rest of a board, set the leftover aside with its number on it. A later step uses it.
  • “16″ apart, center to center” means you measure from the middle of one board to the middle of the next.
0

How it all fits together

The ramp goes together in layers, from the floor up. The drawing pulls the layers apart so you can see each one, and the list under it says what each part is. The steps below build the layers in this order.

ColorsStringers, headers, joists and end headerBlocking and toe blocksLegs, posts and bracesPlywoodCurbsRail posts and handrails
  1. 1
    Legs and postsLegs stand on the slab under the stringers, and posts hold up the platform. Diagonal braces stop them from swaying.16 legs · 6 platform posts · 2 diagonal braces
  2. 2
    FrameStringers are the long boards that run up the slope and carry the deck. Blocks are short boards that fit between the stringers. The platform frame is a box: 2 headers across the ends and joists between them. Toe blocks lie flat on the slab at the low end so the ramp can’t slide. The end header closes off the top of the ramp.8 stringer boards · 12 blocks · 3 toe blocks · 2 platform headers · 5 platform joists · 1 end header
  3. 3
    Plywood deckThe surface you roll on.6 plywood panels
  4. 4
    Curbs2x4s standing on edge along the sides, so wheels can’t roll off.8 curbs
  5. 5
    Handrails4x4 wood posts and the 2x2 rail you hold, with its corners rounded over.28 rail posts · 12 rail pieces · 8 level rail ends

1

Mark the footprint on the slab

  • Clear the area. The whole ramp takes up 17′ 10″ by 17′ 10″. Make sure a door can still swing open and nothing else, like a parked car, is in the way.
  • Mark the outline of each ramp and the platform on the slab with a chalk line, using the drawing below.
  • Check that the platform outline is square: measure from corner to corner both ways. Both should be 7′ 5⅛″. If they are not the same, adjust the lines until they are.
2

Build the platform frame

  • Cut these pieces:
    • 2 headers, each 5′ 3″ long
    • 5 joists, each 5′ long
    • 6 posts, each 5¾″ long
    Open Boards to cut below to see which board each piece comes from.
  • Set a metal post base on the slab at each of the 6 post spots in the drawing, and fasten each one down with 4 concrete screws. Stand a post in each base and screw it in place.
    Close up
  • Build the frame on the floor. Set the 2 headers across the ends and fit the 5 joists between them, 15⅜″ apart, center to center. Screw through the headers into the ends of the 2 outside joists, and hang each of the 3 inside joists on a metal joist hanger at each end.
  • Lift the frame onto the posts. Its top should be 11¼″ above the slab. Check that it is level both ways and square, then fasten each post to its header with 2 metal framing angles, which are L-shaped brackets.
    Close up

3

Cut and build the stringers for Ramp 1

  • Cut these pieces:
    • 4 stringers, each 12′ 1″ long
    • 4 legs, each 2⅞″ long
    Open Boards to cut below to see which board each piece comes from.
  • Cut both ends of each of the 4 stringers at a 4.8° angle, with the two cuts parallel, so the ends stand straight up and down when the stringer sits on its slope. The side view below shows the shape.
  • At the low end, saw a long wedge off the bottom edge of each stringer so it lies flat on the slab for the first 6′ 3¼″. The side view shows the shape.
  • Cut the top of each leg at a 4.8° angle so it sits tight against the sloped stringer.
  • Screw a leg under each stringer at each leg row shown in the side view, with 2 screws, 3″ long, driven at an angle up through the leg into the stringer.

5

Stand the ramps up and add the blocks

  • Cut these pieces:
    • 12 blocks, each 13″ long
    • 3 toe blocks, each 13″ long
    • 2 diagonal braces: 1 at 44¾″ and 1 at 45⅞″
    • 1 end header, 45″ long
    Open Boards to cut below to see which board each piece comes from.
  • Stand the stringers of each ramp up on edge, 14½″ apart, center to center.
  • Where a ramp meets the platform, fasten each stringer end to the platform frame with 2 heavy framing angles.
  • Lay the 3 toe blocks, short 2x4s, flat on the slab between the stringers, 33″ from the low end of Ramp 1. Screw each one to the stringers on both sides, and to the slab with 2 concrete screws, so the ramp can’t slide.
  • Screw the end header across the top end of Ramp 2, and fasten it to whatever the ramp meets there, such as the porch or deck frame.
  • Screw the 12 blocks in between the stringers, where the framing drawing below shows them. Drive 2 screws, 3″ long, into each end of every block, through the board beside it.
  • Under a plywood joint, line the blocks up straight across, so the edges of both plywood panels land on them. Screw straight through the stringer where you can reach the far side, and at an angle where you can’t.
  • At the legs, stagger the blocks: each one sits 3″ farther along the ramp than the one beside it, so you can screw straight through the stringer into both ends of every block. A scrap of 2x4 makes a handy spacer.
  • Screw the 2 diagonal 2x4 braces flat against the rows of legs that are 12″ or taller, one on each row, on the side facing the low end, screwed to every leg each one crosses. They stop the ramp from swaying side to side. No braces are needed along the length, because both ends of each ramp are fastened down.

Lay the plywood deck

  • Cut the 6 plywood panels listed below from 5 sheets of ¾″ plywood, 4 × 8. Cut the narrow panels from the leftovers of the wide ones.
  • Start at the low end. Run a line of construction adhesive along the tops of the boards under the panel, set the panel where the drawing puts it, and screw it down about every 8″ with deck screws.
  • Keep every panel where the drawing puts it. That way each edge lands on a stringer, a joist or a block.
  • At the very low end the plywood sticks out a few inches past the stringers. Sand or plane that front edge to a slope so wheels roll on smoothly.

Install the handrails

  • Cut these pieces:

    Open Boards to cut below to see which board each piece comes from.
  • Bolt each post to the outside of the outer stringer with 2 carriage bolts, standing straight up and down. Check it with a level. Space the posts as the drawing shows, never more than 48″ apart.
  • Near the low end the stringer is too thin to bolt to, so the 6 posts there stand on the slab in post bases held down with concrete screws. Bolt them to the stringer too wherever it is deep enough.
  • Bolt the 8 platform rail posts to the outside of the platform frame the same way.
  • Round over the 4 long corners of every 2x2 rail piece with a ¼″ roundover router bit, or sand them round, so no edge is sharp. This is the part people hold.
  • Fasten the 2x2 rail on top of the posts so the top of the rail is 36″ above the deck. Where two pieces meet, butt them together on top of a post. Drill pilot holes near the ends so the 2x2 doesn’t split.
  • At the top and bottom of each ramp, add a 12″ level piece of 2x2, joined to the sloped rail on top of the end post with an angled cut.
  • Sand the rail smooth so it can’t give anyone a splinter.

    Checks and notes

    Tip. Stringers on Ramp 1 and Ramp 2 come out 12′ 1″ long, just 1″ over a 12′ board. Shorten the run by about 1″ and you can buy the shorter board.

    Side-view drawings stretch the height so the slope is visible. Plan views are to scale.

    How the numbers are worked out
    • Lumber uses real sizes: a 2x6 is 1½ by 5½ inches. Plywood is ¾ inch thick, in 4 by 8 foot sheets.
    • The ramp surface sits on stringers set on edge, 16 inches apart, center to center, with the top of each stringer ¾ inch under the surface.
    • Stringers rest on legs, with no more than 48 inches between supports (36 inches for an electric or bariatric chair). Near the slab the bottom edge of each stringer is trimmed so it lies flat on the slab, and the first leg row starts where the stringers lift off. Leg lengths are measured at the middle of the leg, and the top of each leg is cut at the slope angle.
    • Stringers up to 16 feet are one board. Longer ones are made in pieces that meet over a leg, with a 24 inch splice plate across each joint. Odd and even stringers join over different legs, so the joints are staggered and the ramp has no weak line across it.
    • Outdoors, each row of supports is two posts in concrete or on footings with a beam of two 2x6 plies (three 2x8 plies for an electric or bariatric chair) sitting on top in post caps. Where the ramp is too low for posts, short 4x4 legs stand on concrete pavers, and the low end lies on a gravel and paver pad.
    • Support under the plywood: stringers run the full length about 14 to 16 inches apart, with legs no more than 48 inches apart under them. Blocking sits at every leg row and at every plywood joint across the ramp. On decks wider than 48 inches the long seam is moved onto a stringer. On the platform the seam is moved onto a joist, with blocking where a seam crosses the joists. For a heavy power chair, ask a builder about closer stringers or thicker plywood.
    • Chair type: manual uses stringers 16 inches apart and legs every 48 inches. Electric or bariatric tightens that to 12 inches and 36 inches, raises the stringers to 2x8, uses 4x4 legs, and asks for a clear width of 42 inches or more. With the ADA box checked it also makes the platform at least 6 feet clear inside the curbs.
    • Handrails: wood is a 2x2 rail with its corners rounded over, on 4x4 wood posts; metal is 1¼ inch galvanized pipe on pipe posts with slip-on fittings. Either way the rail is 36 inches above the deck on posts bolted to the outside of the stringers about every 4 feet. Each rail runs level for 12 inches past the top and bottom of a ramp. Platform edges get rails only when you pick both sides.
    • The curbs are 2x4s on edge, screwed on top of the deck at both edges. Deck width is the clear width plus 3 inches.
    • Lumber counts come from packing every cut into 8 to 16 foot boards, then shrinking each board to the shortest stock length that still holds its cuts. Buy one or two extra boards for mistakes.
    • Code mode: the Code check measures the ramp against the common ADA figures (1:12 slope, 30 inches of rise per run, 60 inch landings, 36 inch width, rails 34 to 38 inches high, 2 inch curbs). Turning the mode on holds the slope at 1:12 or gentler, puts rails on both sides, and makes a turning platform at least 5 feet clear inside the curbs (6 feet for an electric or bariatric chair). With it off, the platform is the size you type, as long as the ramps fit on it. The Quote section makes a materials estimate from the starting prices you edit; tick Full quote to add your labor, markup, deposit and terms. Nothing is sent anywhere. Saved jobs and prices stay in this browser.
    • This is a planning tool. It is not engineered, and it does not check a chair and rider against your lumber. For a heavy power chair or a tall platform, have someone qualified look at the design.
